en: The Ritual for Cultivation and Realization at the Śūraṃgama Maṇḍala, compiled by the Jinshui Śramaṇa Jingyuan. Preface:
The Great Śūraṃgama Sūtra is the essential gateway through which the nine realms of existence converge, and the wondrous point of profound union with the One Vehicle.
This is the Way. To recite incantations, he surrounded the altar for six periods; to verify the realization of the fruits, he sat in meditation for a hundred days.
Although these were ritual observances, they were profound and subtle; in truth, they were a clear illumination through contemplation of principle.

As for cultivating the three contemplations to harmonize the seven elements, and expelling demonic realms while traversing the stages of sainthood, even the commentaries of recent antiquity state that these matters are fully provided therein. At the beginning of the Jingyou era...
(Jingyuan) has humbly received this sutra from the Master of the Changshui Commentary and from the gate of the Venerable of Jin-yun.
Although I have studied to establish my resolve and contemplated to consolidate the Way, I have merely endeavored to excerpt the profound meanings and compile abridged commentaries.
As for the grand regulations for establishing boundaries and reciting mantras, as well as the elegant models for the sequence of ritual invocations, I have not yet [dealt with them].

I have found leisure to take up the pen. In the fourth year of the Xining era, while teaching the Way at the Baoge Monastery on Qingdun, amidst my instructions to others, I examined various commentaries such as those by Changshui and Gushan, as well as the transcriptions by Jinheng, Wenxun, and others.

Having extensively gathered the standards of the ritual platforms and sought afar for the protocols of the ceremonial arrangements, I edited and revised the merits of the earnest vows and compiled the essentials of the repentance rites—all of which...

In all cases, I have examined the texts and scrutinized the facts, analyzing their similarities and differences. This was also in response to the repeated requests of the scholars of our own school (Zongli).

Thus, while my elegant compositions and grand rhetoric fall far short of those of the former sages, I hope that by promoting goodness and distancing myself from transgression, I shall not be ashamed before future generations.
The ritual procedures for practicing repentance are briefly explained in ten parts:
first, the layout and regulations of the altar site; second, the invocation of the worthy and holy ones; third, the gate of visualization for making offerings.
Fourth, praising the Tathāgata; fifth, paying homage to the Triple Gem; sixth, chanting mantras around the altar;
seventh, purifying karmic obstructions according to the prescribed methods; eighth, repenting and making vows; ninth, circumambulating while reciting.

Tenth: The method of analytical and comprehensive contemplation of the Dharma. (As for the methods for purifying the body, they are fully detailed in the two manuals of repentance, the *Xingyuan* and the *Chanyuan*; I hope that all students will examine them in detail and receive the ancestral instructions therein).
Chapter One: The Square Regulations of the Altar Site.
In the past, our Buddha, the Great Sage, observed that the transgressions of ordinary people arise easily; he held that only through stillness can their fundamental natures be governed.
Consequently, the ritual protocols for Buddhist monasteries (*brahmacarya*) were mostly established in deep, secluded mountain valleys and remote forests and springs. Since...
Being far removed from the inhabitants, the dust of bustling crowds does not startle them, and the rattle of heavy carts does not reach them.
Neither falsehood nor guile can move their hearts, nor can right and wrong entangle their minds. Once the mind and heart are thus tranquil, one may hope to advance along the Way.

Now, regarding the establishment of the altar for this sutra: since there are neither the Snowy Mountains nor white oxen here, one should follow the sutra by simply selecting yellow earth from beneath five feet of surface soil on a level plain and mixing it with sandalwood, aloeswood, and *sugandha* incense.
Frankincense, saffron, white resin, *candana* (sandalwood), *linglang*, *gansong*, and *jiheshang* (the origins of these incense names are detailed in the *Continued Han Shu* and the *Yiwuzhi*).
These ten types of incense were finely ground into powder and mixed with earth to form a paste, which was then applied to the site of the altar (*guoyu* states: "the ground cleared for the altar").

[It is] called a *cháng* (field). It is sixteen feet square and circular, serving as an octagonal altar (*tán*). (Zheng Xuan’s commentary on the *Lǐjì* states: "To enclose earth is called an altar (*tán*). "To enclose" means to raise the boundaries of the earth.

This means that one first clears the ground to make a *cháng*, and subsequently takes yellow earth, mixes it with incense to form mud, and applies this mud upon the *cháng* to raise it into the form of an altar. The dimensions of its height and depth may be determined according to one's intention based on the quantity of ritual implements. Ancient practitioners took two feet for each corner, totaling sixteen feet (2 x 8 = 16) to constitute sixteen feet. The *Jíjiě* (Collected Explanations) considers this too narrow;

one should instead take the diameter to be sixteen feet, as in the *Fāngděng xíngfǎ* (Method of Practice for the Vaipulya), which also instructs the construction of an altar measuring one zhang and six chi in length and breadth). At the center of the altar, place...

A lotus flower made of gold, silver, copper, or wood (or one carved from wood and overlaid with thin sheets of gold or silver, according to what is appropriate) should be used to decorate the casket and contain the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which is placed before the lotus.

Within the flower, place an alms bowl (either dark blue or white porcelain bowls are also acceptable). First, fill the bowl with dew collected in the eighth month (at other times, simply use pure water).
Place whatever flowers and leaves are available within the water. Then, take eight round mirrors and place each of them [in their respective positions].

Squarely surrounding the flower bowl, sixteen lotus flowers and sixteen incense burners are established outside the mirror, interspersed with floral arrangements and adorned with incense burners that burn only aloeswood so that the flame is not visible. Take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels;
prepare milk pancakes along with various granulated sugars, oil cakes, milk porridge, storax, honey-ginger, pure ghee, and pure [milk products].
Honey. Outside the lotus flowers, there are sixteen [offerings] surrounding each flower on the outside, presented to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
At every mealtime, or at midnight, take half a *sheng* of honey and three *he* of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
In front of the altar, separately set up a small fire hearth. Boil *turuṣka* incense (formerly called "white mugwort") to extract scented water, and bathe [the image].
Charcoal. Light it until it blazes fiercely, then cast this ghee and honey into the flaming furnace, burning them until no smoke remains.

Offer this to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas (the term "xiang" means to present or offer). Hang banners and flowers everywhere around the four sides [of the altar] (regarding offerings to the Sages, seek out whatever is available in each direction; one must strive daily to provide all that is required to hope for spiritual assistance.

If one’s resources are insufficient, it is permitted to proceed from the first day until the end, gradually accumulating one's surplus wealth to extend one’s sincere devotion). Within the four walls of the ritual chamber, spread...
If one establishes images of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas, they should be positioned facing forward.

One should display images of Vairocana, Śākyamuni, Maitreya, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and various great transformational forms of Avalokiteśvara, along with Vajragarbha, installed at their left and right sides.
Furthermore, Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, and Lambaka, as well as the various Mañjughoṣas...

[The images of] Śrī, Viṣkumbhin, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Pāñcika (translated from Sanskrit into Chinese; the meaning is found in various texts) shall be displayed at the sides of the gate, installed on the left and right.

Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them inverted in the air, so that they face the mirrors installed within the maṇḍala courtyard, with their surfaces opposite one another, causing their forms and reflections to interpenetrate in successive layers. During the first seven days, [one should] pay homage with utmost sincerity.

Pay homage to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and those titled Arhats. Constantly, throughout the six periods of the day and night, recite mantras around the altar and practice the Way with a sincere heart.
At each session, constantly perform one hundred and eight recitations (regarding the ritual for the number of mantra recitations, see the text below).
Second, during the seven days, focus your mind single-mindedly to make Bodhisattva vows without interruption. In my Vinaya, there are already established vows.

(The instructions are as found in the *Jin heng chao* [Golden Balance Manuscript]). During the third week, at all twelve periods of the day, one should single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s *Bhadrakarātrī* mantra.
On the seventh day, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will simultaneously appear at the place where the mirrors reflect one another's light, and the Buddha will touch one’s head with his hand.
...up until: after twenty-one days have passed, one sits upright in retreat for one hundred days. Those of sharp faculties may attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* without rising from their seats;
even if their bodies and minds remain unrestrained and the holy fruit is not yet fully realized, they will certainly know for themselves that their attainment of Buddhahood is unerring.

(Regarding the construction of the altar and the cultivation of skillful means and correct practice: it is appropriate to commence these on the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*). As for the ritual procedures for worship and recitation—if one were to follow the scriptural texts entirely in establishing the altar and paying homage, it would indeed be a difficult task. However, [the essential points are as follows]...)

One should act according to the specific circumstances and proceed according to one's own capacity; in principle, there should be no fault. However, since we are far removed from the Sage and those who follow the teachings are increasingly few, if one were to insist on waiting for all conditions to be perfectly fulfilled before performing ritual recitation, it would cause those who have not yet practiced to despair and abandon their efforts out of sight of the goal. This statement is well-founded.
I have previously extracted [this essence] and focused it specifically here, intending to inform those who come after. Section Two: Invoking the Sages and Worthies.

The Patriarch of the Ruyong Repentance, whose fundamental realization is wondrous enlightenment, is named *Saddharmaprabha* (Zhengfaming); in his provisional manifestation, he dwells as one on the verge of Buddhahood and is called Avalokiteśvara (*Guanshiyin*).

Those who practice this rite, upon first entering the ritual arena, should recite the Honored One’s name and circumambulate once. Arriving before the altar or the Dharma seat, they shall spread out their *niṣīdana* (sitting cloth), stand upright with bodies aligned, and give rise to a heart of profound sincerity and reverence.

I entreat the Triple Gem. Although all Buddhas and sages are omnipresent, if one lacks sincerity, their invocation will fail to move them to descend. Therefore, this sutra states that during the first seven days, by reverently prostrating to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, they shall suddenly appear simultaneously within the space where mirrors reflect one another's light.
Receiving the Buddhas' touch upon the crown of the head, one may then cultivate *samādhi* within the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).

This enables those who study and practice in such a degenerate age to purify body and mind until they are as clear and transparent as lapis lazuli. Now, you should single-mindedly refrain from distraction; prostrate with your five limbs touching the ground, raise your three points [the knees and forehead], and fix your mind and gaze upon the visualization.
[The Master of Repentance leads the invocation:
"With all reverence, with a single mind, we prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm.

(Having performed this general prostration to the Triple Gem once, those kneeling with palms joined hold the incense burner and burn various named incenses to respectfully invite the worthy sages and saints. For those practicing alone, omit the first four characters and simply prostrate to the Triple Gem. According to the *Ritual for the Repentance of Perfect Enlightenment*, one always first invites [the deities] and subsequently makes offerings. However, as for the ritual text...)

Regarding the invocation of Vairocana: his image is displayed within the maṇḍala. The commentary also states: "As for the *Abhiṣeka* section, it consists of five families (*pañcakula*); this [text] corresponds to one of them, with Vairocana as its presiding lord."
With single-minded devotion, I reverently entreat: Homage to the Great Maṇḍala Sūtra; to the Lord of the Consecration Division;
to Vairocana Buddha, in whom wisdom and principle are perfectly integrated. (Three times entreat, once prostrate; hereafter follow this pattern.)

With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat Śākyamuni Buddha, who proclaims the dhāraṇī from the Light upon the Crown; and all the Buddhas, as numerous as atoms, who equally demonstrate the cycle of rebirth and liberation of the six sense faculties.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in and entreat the Honored Buddha Maitreya, who will descend in the future age; Akṣobhya of the East; and [the Buddha] of the West.
I single-mindedly entreat the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, as well as all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time:
Homage to the Buddha’s Crown Radiance-Gathering, the Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the King of Śūraṅgama Samādhi,
who is fully endowed with the myriad practices, and to all the true and pure Dharma-treasures of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva of the Secret Retention Mantra, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva who has entered the Samādhi of Reality,
the twenty-four sages who together expounded the Perfect Penetration, and all the provisional and ultimate Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha-rāja, who constantly follows the heart-mantra; the incalculable bodhisattvas who seek the secret meaning;
and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

With single-minded devotion, we pay homage: Namo to the Venerable Ānanda, who expounded the wondrous teachings; to the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, who illuminated the nature and characteristics of phenomena;
and to all the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Saṅgha within the entire assembly of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra.
With single-minded devotion, we offer this invocation: Homage to those who have made vows with utmost sincerity to protect practitioners—
the Brahmā and Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, the Sun and Moon Devas, the various palaces and stellar luminaries, the deities of wind and rain,
as well as the presiding and governing spirits within this realm, the deities who guard the site of practice in this dwelling place, and all worthy sages who uphold the True Dharma.
[This stage involves only three requests; one should not perform prostrations. There is no hindrance for laypeople.

The Third Gate of Offering and Contemplation (based on the sutra: fill a bowl with water and place various flowers and leaves within it). According to the *Mahāsamaya-samudra Sūtra*, one should offer flowers of grass and trees held in the hands;

the wording is largely the same. That people nowadays, when practicing repentance, mostly offer flowers made of colored silk is likely because they encounter times of frost and snow. At other times, one should seek to follow the sutra. When making offerings to the Triple Gem, one should...
One should collect the mind and look upward with devotion, thinking: "May the Buddhas and the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles not fail my request.

While abiding in their own samādhis, may they arise from that concentration through the resonance of their compassion, responding to my karmic conditions so as to fill the ritual arena and pervade the realm of empty space. May they know and behold our visualization and offerings. Then, the Sound-Virtue (Śabdaguṇa) practitioner holds the incense burner and proclaims:

These various assemblies each knelt with one knee on the ground and, solemnly holding incense and flowers, made offerings according to the Dharma (at this point, the chanting ceased; they held the flowers aloft with their hands).

One should form a mental image and recite silently as follows: "The pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas possesses immeasurable merit; it neither abides nor perishes, but remains serene and eternally peaceful. The incense and flowers that I hold are all produced from grasses and trees;

I offer them to all Buddhas, maintaining this visualization as my offering. From every pore of my body, may countless incense and flowers emerge from each and every pore, vowing to make offerings to all Buddhas. May these transform into platforms of incense and flowers. Once the Buddhas have accepted them, may they perform Buddha-works throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

These shall then return and become golden platforms, remaining before us. Having completed this visualization, one scatters flowers and again takes up the incense burner, uttering these sincere words: "May these incense and flowers fill the ten directions..."
Throughout the ten directions, I make offerings to all Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas, as well as the assemblies of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

I pray that all Tathāgatas, in places where mirror-images and light-reflecting shadows interpenetrate, will accept these clouds of incense and flowers to serve as luminous altars, pervading boundless realms and performing immeasurable Buddha-works.

(The above is largely based on the intent of the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, with two lines from the root scripture added to complete the altar ritual and to introduce the subsequent text. Furthermore, previously...

The verses within the commentary consist of eighteen lines; these are also the prose sections of that sutra. Here, I have merely extracted the essential meaning and composed them as verses, desiring that practitioners may silently recite and contemplate them without omission. If one practices this for oneself, omit the eight characters "除是諸眾等" (excluding these various assemblies), and understand the rest by this analogy.

For the line beginning with "無量" (Immeasurable), the entire assembly joins in harmony. For the seven characters beginning with "供養" (Making offerings), the Master of Sound and Virtue chants them himself. Having made offerings, all pay homage with reverence (rising to perform one prostration).

Praising the Tathāgata, Part Four: Having completed the offerings, one next rectifies one’s deportment and bows deeply to praise the subtle and wondrous merits of all Buddhas. One must also visualize clearly;
only then will the praiser and the praised be as mirror and reflection, interpenetrating one another in successive layers.
O Wondrous, Profound, and All-Holding Lord of Immovability, The King of Śūraṅgama Samādhi, rare in this world!
Eradicate my inverted thoughts accumulated over billions of kalpas; Without passing through the aeons of saṃgha, protect my Dharma-body.
May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, To once again deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
With this profound resolve, I shall serve all lands as numerous as motes of dust; this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to bear witness: I vow to enter first into the evil lands of the five turbidities.
As long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall never enter nirvana here.
O Great Hero, of Great Power and Great Compassion, I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtle delusions,
So that I may quickly ascend to Unsurpassed Enlightenment.
Even if the nature of Śūnyatā (the void) were to perish throughout the worlds of the ten directions, My diamond-like mind shall never waver.
[Having finished the praise, one should now state the purpose of practicing the repentance. If there is a specific prayer, it should be set forth here with truthful words.

The Fifth Section: Paying Homage to the Triple Gem Having completed the eulogy, one should single-mindedly recollect the true bodies of all Buddhas, which manifest forms in accordance with sentient beings as if they were standing before one's very eyes.

Accept my prostrations. Furthermore, you should know that body and mind are empty and quiescent; there is no mark of salutation. Appearing as reflections according to conditions, this very body is present before each and every Buddha, bowing its head in reverent salutation.

According to the explanation of Tripitaka Master Paramārtha, there are seven types of prostration. Master Qingliang added three more to make ten. 1. **Prostration of Pride**: Like a pestle moving up and down, it is performed without a heart of reverence. 2. **Prostration of Chanting and Harmony**: Performed with loud voices and clamor, where words and phrases are confused and disordered.

These two are not in accordance with the ritual. 3. **Prostration of Reverence**: The five wheels (the two knees, two elbows, and forehead) touch the ground; one reverently supports the feet with gravity. 4. **Prostration of Non-characteristic**:

One enters deeply into the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), transcending the characteristics of subject and object. 5. **Prostration of Manifesting Function**: Although there is no subject or object, one universally mobilizes body and mind so that they pervade everywhere like a shadow, worshipping that which cannot be worshipped. 6. **Prostration of Internal Contemplation**: One worships only the dharmas within the body.

The body is the true Buddha; do not seek it outwardly. First is the prostration of the seven real marks (*saptalakṣaṇa*), wherein the internal and external are one and the same reality. Second is the prostration of the eight great compassions (*mahākaruṇā*), which, with each individual prostration, universally takes the place of all sentient beings.

Third is the prostration of universal inclusion, which subsumes the preceding six gates into a single contemplation. Fourth is the inexhaustible prostration, which enters the realm of the Indra’s net (*indrājāla*); whether regarding the Buddhas or the prostrations themselves, they are infinitely layered and inexhaustible.

According to the scriptural text, one should "with utmost sincerity prostrate to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions," appearing simultaneously in the place where mirrors reflect one another's light and receiving the Buddhas' touch upon the crown of the head. Interpreting this through the meaning of the commentary, one correctly distinguishes the fifth and tenth [prostrations]. Truly.
I prostrate with single-minded devotion to the latter eight [sections].
I prostrate with single-minded devotion to the Great Maṇḍala Sūtra, the Lord of the Consecration Division, the Buddha Vairocana, in whom principle and wisdom are perfectly integrated.
I prostrate with single-minded devotion to Śākyamuni Buddha, who, from within his uṣṇīṣa, radiates hundreds of jewel-lights and proclaims this divine mantra.

With single-minded devotion, we prostrate. We proclaim with one voice: liberation from saṃsāra depends entirely upon the six sense faculties. All the Buddhas, as numerous as motes of dust, prostrate with single-minded devotion.
Abiding in the four heavens, they manifest the eight phases of enlightenment. This shall apply to the Honored Buddha Maitreya when he descends to be born in the future.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to Akṣobhya of the East and Amitāyus of the West, as well as to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya, the Supreme Jewel Seal, and these secret gāthās of subtle and wondrous syllables.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. The Tathāgata has revealed the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the King of Samādhis, which is the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization;
it is fully endowed with the myriad practices and all the true, pure Dharma-treasures of the ten directions.

With single-minded devotion, he prostrated himself and secretly upheld the divine mantras; furthermore, he inquired about the true vision and selected the Perfect Penetration of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who, through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, entered true samādhi; who wondrously accords with the capacities of all beings;

who, in harmony with others, expounded the perfect penetration, extinguishing dust to unite with awakening and turning back the faculties to return to their original nature—to all these holy assemblies, I prostrate with single-minded devotion.
With single-minded devotion, we pay homage. All have described their cultivation and realization. As the profound consciousness follows its source, it returns to be identical with the fundamental.
With single-minded devotion, all the assembly of holy ones pays homage. Constantly following the heart-mantra, Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattva seeks the secret meaning.
Together with Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. To him who manifested his traces at the Śūraṅgama Assembly to reveal the delusion of the true, and who expounded the wondrous teaching—to the Venerable Ānanda, with single-minded devotion, I pay homage.
To him who opened up the clarity of nature and characteristics—to the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.

To all those within the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* who have excellently transcended all realms of existence—the śrāvakas of no-more-learning, as well as the countless pratyekabuddhas and noble saṃgha of the initial resolve. With single-minded devotion, I pay homage.

Section Six: Chanting Mantras and Circumambulating the Altar (This section cites the scripture and concludes it; alternatively, one may follow the ritual manual for recitation, though with slight differences in vocalization).

The Scripture states: "Constantly, during the six periods [of the day], chant mantras while circumambulating the altar" (this first indicates practicing the path and chanting mantras during the six periods).

"Practice the path with a sincere mind, performing this at all times, one hundred and eight times per period" (this next explains the number of repetitions for each period of practice). Examining this text further, it appears to refer approximately to the first seven days.
One encircles the altar and recites the mantra. As stated in the commentary, for each session one should recite it one hundred and eight times;
this refers specifically to the recitation of this Heart Mantra. Those who now practice this cultivation need not be restricted to ten people.

If one practices this method of repentance at the beginning of the new year or prior to the holy festival, one may set a limit of seven days, or proceed as one’s capacity allows, or on the third and eighth days of the month.
As the assembly of monks is large, they may collectively recite the mantra once before the altar or the Dharma seat (the method for reciting the mantra is detailed in Master Ciyun’s *Niansong Yi*;

this text should also be recited in a forceful voice so that the sound remains uninterrupted). The words of the mantra are as in the seventh sutra. (Once the prostrations to the Buddhas have been completed, next adjust your robes and sit cross-legged in the manner of one in meditative concentration;
however, those who possess a resonant voice shall kneel facing each other and hold the incense burner, saying:)
Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṃgha; homage to Śākyamuni Buddha;
homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (Having recited this three times, next raise the sutra:
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed Ānanda, saying: "If there are sentient beings whose past karmic deeds have not yet been eliminated..."

Instruct this person to single-mindedly recite and maintain the Buddha’s Crown Light Mantra. This is the unconditioned heart-Buddha of the Tathāgata, who radiates light from his crown and sits upon a precious lotus flower.
Recite the heart-mantra he has spoken (either seven times, fourteen times, or up to one hundred and eight times, according to the occasion and whether the practice is extensive or abbreviated).
Tadyathā (1) Oṃ (2) Anale (3) Viśati (4) Vīravajradhāri (5) Bandha bandhani (6) Vajrabandhini Phaṭ (7) Hūṃ dhuruṃ phaṭ (8) Svāhā (9). (Having finished reciting the mantra,
the reciter of the sūtra kneels again with legs crossed, holding the incense burner and forming the mudrā.)

The Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who, since beginningless time, have committed all manner of light and heavy karmic obstacles, which they have not yet had the opportunity to repent for from previous lives—if they are able to read and recite [this],..."
The various sins committed since beginningless time by one who possesses the bodhicitta are like [a vast ocean].
There is no sin that is not exhausted; therefore, one must, before the Three Jewels, repent and reproach one's former mind, confessing all transgressions. Regarding grave offenses (āpatti):

if the preparatory intention is heavy, and both at the time of committing and after having committed it, the three times [of preparation, execution, and completion] are all heavy, such that the mind and the object correspond, and furthermore, it constitutes a heinous crime (ānantarya).

As for sins: those who slander the Vaipulya sutras, the icchantikas, and others who commit numerous acts of profit while being deluded regarding causes and mistaken about effects—failing to recognize their transgressions and failing to recognize the Dharma—are termed "high-grade" (upamāna).

Regarding "medium-grade" (madhyama) sins: these involve the actual performance of an act through skillful means, where the mind is heavy during the two stages of preparation and execution, yet light after the act is completed;
or where the object is heavy but the mind is subtle; or where the three factors [of object, mind, and effort] are not extreme; or where the acts are frequent but not numerous, and one is not deluded.
The middle grade of offenses is defined by their causes and effects. Regarding the minor grade of offenses: the preceding and succeeding mental states are grave, while the act itself is light;
the object of the offense contradicts the intention, and it is not an offense committed against the monastic community. Furthermore, they are few in number and do not bring harm;

one recognizes the Dharma and recognizes the transgression, clearly understanding cause and effect—this is called the minor grade. Now, for those who wish to repent of these three grades of offenses, there are three gates of repentance. The first is subduing.
There are three types of repentance for karma: first, the repentance for subduing karma; second, the repentance for transforming karma; and third, the repentance for extinguishing karma.

Regarding what is called "subduing" (*vinaya*): it refers to repenting according to the specific teachings of the Three Vehicles. For the first four categories of offenses, one merely subdues them so that they do not arise; this is termed "repentance.

Once the disclosure has been made, the original offense does not increase, and there are no further offenses such as concealment or hiding. That which should have arisen does not arise; this is termed "subduing. Second is the transformation of karma.

This means: by exchanging a short period for a long period, and by using light suffering to suppress heavy suffering, one vows that whatever retribution should be experienced within the three evil realms shall instead be repaid in this present body, rather than being received in those evil realms; this is called the repentance for transforming karma. Third, regarding the elimination of karma:
one must have clear understanding through contemplation and insight, and deeply resolve to generate the great Bodhicitta. Regarding all that has been created since beginningless time...
All transgressions are like a dark room; repentance through right wisdom is likened to a bright lamp. When the bright lamp shines once, all gloom is dispelled;

the darkness cannot resist the lamp, no matter how great it may be. Due to delusion as the cause and error as the fruit, one commits every kind of fault, and the Buddha-nature remains hidden, thus resembling a dark room.
When the fire of true wisdom is ignited, it is equivalent to the bright lamp: as the lamp arises, the darkness is removed, and liberation is born.

Delusions are lost; there is no karma that will not be extinguished. I pray that all practitioners shall examine their own transgressions and give rise to the resolve to repent and cleanse them, relying solely upon right wisdom.

Chapter Eight: Repentance and Making Vows (Having understood that there are three grades of offenses and three gates of repentance, next, with a focused mind, maintaining upright posture and dignified demeanor, one should kneel respectfully.)

Burn various famous incenses and visualize Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, adorned with immeasurable ornaments and surrounded by a retinue, presiding as the master of the confession, as if standing before one's eyes. Confess and reveal all transgressions committed throughout immeasurable kalpas.

Regarding all evil karma previously committed, one cuts off the continuity of the mind and shall not create it again; rather, with right wisdom, one contemplates that the nature of sin is empty, abiding neither within nor without, and reverently gives rise to the great bodhicitta.

To utterly destroy the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one should single-mindedly recite these words: "For all the karmic obstructions of sin committed by myself and all sentient beings since beginningless time, I pray that the Triple Gem will compassionately rescue us.

May our evil karma be instantly dispelled and transformed into pure causes; may body and mind be equally empty, and may sin and merit have no master. May we clearly perceive true nature and become equal to the Dharma-body of the Buddhas;

may the transgressions of the three karmas become the three gates of liberation, and may the heavy obscurations of the six sense faculties be transformed into the six supernormal powers. Having recited this, chant: ( )
For the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*, I vow that all obstacles shall be severed and eliminated.

Having chanted this, rise and perform one prostration. One should then cultivate the ten minds of contrition and compliance, reciting the Verse of Qingliang as follows: "Since beginningless time, ignorance has arisen; I have also encountered evil friends who increased my afflictions. Lacking a heart of sympathetic joy, my goodness was forever extinguished;

Though I spoke and thought, evils gradually took birth. Mind upon mind, they spread everywhere, defiling every place touched; Thought after thought, they continued in succession, active day and night. I did not wish for others to know, concealing my transgressions; I feared not the evil paths, acting with reckless abandon. Without shame and without remorse, the Māra..."

The Net: Pushing aside both cause and effect, one falls into the pit of the icchantika. Having thus followed the current and turned one's back on the source, the ocean of birth-and-death misery overflows vast and boundless. Fortunately, you, son of a noble householder, recognize its origin; now you wish to go against the current and abandon the poor village. With right faith in cause and effect, you break the icchantika;

with shame and remorse, you break the shameless among gods and humans; by fearing the evil realms, you break the fearless; by confessing sinful karma, you break concealment; by severing the mind of continuity, you break constant attachment; by generating the bodhicitta, you break pervasive arising; by cultivating merit to compensate for faults, you break self-indulgence; by guarding the true Dharma, you break joylessness;

by mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions, you break evil friends; and by contemplating the emptiness of the nature of sin, you break the fetters and afflictions. Of the six preceding verses, the first three concern the ten minds that follow birth-and-death as the objects to be remedied, while the latter three concern the reversal of birth-and-death.
The ten minds: these should be recited and silently contemplated in reverse order. Then, speak as follows: With a sincere heart, I repent.
I, Bhikṣu [Name], and others, take refuge in the inexhaustible Triple Gem of the ten directions. We pray that you will arise with compassion and act as our witness.

From beginningless time, I and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm have continued in the cycle of birth and death because we were ignorant of the eternally abiding true mind and its intrinsically pure nature.

The essence is luminous, yet it employs various delusive thoughts. Because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic existence; from confusion to further confusion, one passes through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
Fortunately, by virtue of roots of goodness, one is born among humans and receives the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni’s Semblance Dharma.

Though the body has left the household life, the mind does not enter the Way; one violates the prohibitive precepts and destroys the essence of the fundamental precepts. Furthermore, mired in dullness and distraction, one fails to practice cultivation.

Regarding concentration and wisdom: it is only now that we have begun to awaken to the fact that we are entangled by the two obstacles. This is truly because we do not know the nature of the mind, which is quiescent and eternal.
We further reflect that, together with all sentient beings, we are moved by our own karma; having created the ten habitual causes, we undergo the sixfold intersecting retributions.

These begin with the habit of lust, wherein the reception of thoughts forms the womb, and end with the cause of litigation, wherein clamorous disputes and concealment prevail. This is all due to the six consciousnesses of sentient beings.
We have created karma that issues from the six sense faculties; thus, each has individually drawn forth evil retributions.
We shall surely fall into the three miserable realms, where we will undergo all manner of suffering for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, unable to escape or end it.

We pray that our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, the Universal Savior and Master of Repentance, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and the others, will take pity on us who are drowning in the sea of suffering and skillfully lead us out by their compassionate hands. We pray...

I accept your confession. May you emerge from the ocean of suffering. Through the merit of my confession regarding the faculty of the eye, I vow that this eye shall see through to the pure *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions, without perceiving them through dualistic marks.

Through the merit of my confession regarding the faculty of the ear, I vow that this ear shall constantly hear the true Dharma spoken by all Buddhas, worthies, and sages throughout the ten directions, as if...

I shall teach and cause this to be practiced. By the merit of my repentance regarding the faculty of the nose, I vow that this nose shall always smell the fragrance of the Accumulated Merit (Gandhavyūha) that enters the station of Dharma, and shall abandon the impure stench and filth of birth and death.

By the merit of my repentance regarding the faculty of the tongue, I vow that this tongue shall always partake of the food of the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna, and shall not crave the flavors of the flesh and blood of sentient beings. I...

Regarding the merit of the faculty of body that I have repented, I vow that this body shall don the robes of the Tathāgata, wear the armor of patience, lie upon the bed of fearlessness, and sit upon the seat of the four dhyānas.

Regarding the merit of the faculty of mind that I have repented, I vow that this mind shall accomplish the ten perceptions, penetrate the five sciences, and deeply contemplate the principle of the equality of emptiness within the two truths. Furthermore, we vow to offer...
By upholding this divine mantra, one shall rescue and protect the world, attaining great fearlessness. Devas and nāgas will rejoice; wind and rain will follow their proper seasons;

the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad people will be wealthy and long-lived. Holy emperors and enlightened kings will be endowed with both benevolence and majesty; the five nobles and hundreds of officials will all cultivate loyalty and filial piety;
and teachers, monks, parents, and lay patrons alike—regardless of whether they are friends or enemies, or beings of the hidden or manifest realms—all shall [attain peace].
One gives rise to the fourfold faith and awakens the bodhicitta.

By relying on these subtle and wondrous phrases of the dhāraṇī-heart, all karmic obstructions accumulated over vast eons—such accumulated karma—is like ice melting in boiling water; before long, one shall fully realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Having completed the repentance and made the vows, take refuge and pay homage to the Triple Gem. (This text for repentance, as well as the invocations to the various saints, must be recited in advance so that one is thoroughly proficient in them.

If one proceeds through the text while circumambulating within the ritual arena, the mind will lack sincerity; how then could there be a descent of spiritual response to seek the extinction of transgressions? Furthermore, regarding the verses for scattering flowers and other such passages, there are separate printed editions available;
those who wish to perform these practices should recite them silently.)
Circumambulating while reciting the ninth [verse]:
Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions; homage to the Dharma of the ten directions; homage to the Sangha of the ten directions;
homage to the Lord of the Sūtra at the Site of Enlightenment, Vairocana Buddha.
Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, who proclaims the mantra from the Light of the Crown;
homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions whose light of teaching universally pervades;
homage to the Mahābuddhōṣṇīṣa-Śūraṅgama Sūtra.
Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, the Secret Holder of Divine Mantras;
homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the Master of Repentance of Universal Penetration;
homage to the Bodhisattvas who have equally realized the provisional and the ultimate through cultivation.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who seek the profound meaning;
homage to all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the ten directions.

(As for those who circumambulate to the right, they proceed in a clockwise direction with deep reverence, gazing [upon the object] insatiably. Thus, they perform three circumambulations, or even up to a hundred, though there is no fixed number. Next, regarding the recitation of Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration of the Virtue of Sound, it is stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "Avalokiteśvara... )

Regarding the Bodhisattva Sound’s Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration: if one practices the ritual of a single session, merely reciting the sutras within the ritual arena for a period limited to seven days, one must establish a separate hall for dhyāna meditation outside the ritual arena before entering the altar.
Having completed the confession, one should immediately recite the sutras in this hall (the rules for chanting the sutras are also explained in the *Bhadracaryā-vidhi*).
This concludes the tenth section, "The Method of Analytical Contemplation.
Some may say that mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) is indeed the root of internal practice and the essential path for the Three Vehicles; yet, regarding the present ritual of confession...

"Why do you not comply? He replied: "Now, regarding the establishment of the contemplation of dharmas, there is the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) and the gate that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-mukha*).

Skillful means is restricted to partial cultivation, whereas that which accords with reality is universal for complete realization. Although this sutra contains the skillful means of counting the breaths, it is restricted and not universal;
thus it was superseded by Mañjuśrī. Therefore, the sutra says: 'The mental visualization of the nose is fundamentally a provisional device (*upāya-kauśalya*),' and so forth."

This causes the mind to be gathered and abide; once abiding is achieved, it becomes the state wherein the mind dwells. How does one attain perfect penetration? (In the sutra text, there are accounts based on the sense organs and consciousnesses; here, only one is cited.)
If one speaks of the actual, perfect realization that is pervasive and not limited, it is precisely what is bestowed by Avalokiteśvara (Miaode).
Thus, the Sūtra says: "The true essence of the teaching in this realm is pure within sound and hearing; those who wish to enter samādhi truly enter through the midst of hearing.

(The commentary further explains: Once the essence of the teaching is established, one then contemplates and practices until entering samādhi and achieving great liberation. Since the school takes the single gate of Avalokiteśvara as supreme, from [this point]...
Other various skillful means are not to be practiced for long; this is precisely why I do not include the counting of breaths [in my primary teaching].

How much more so when one establishes a method as a model for practice to guide and benefit those with karmic affinity—by paying homage, visiting, and making offerings, the merit is equal to that of sixty-two billion *koṭis* of *paramāṇus* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* bodhisattvas;
how could it be fully described? If one were to speak according to reality, it encompasses all directions...

Thus, counting the breaths also cultivates both the gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). In this present sutra, the gate of the binding and unbinding of faculties and objects determines the cultivation of *śamatha*;
the gate of the identity and difference of cause and effect determines the cultivation of *vipaśyanā*.

Should a practitioner, while performing various ritual acts within the *maṇḍala*, give rise to even a fleeting deluded thought, they lose *śamatha*. If for a moment they forget their illuminating awareness, they lack [the necessary conditions].
Regarding contemplation: if this is so, then only when stillness and illumination flow together and cessation and contemplation operate in tandem can it be considered correct cultivation;
all other ritual procedures are merely auxiliary practices.
